newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German business tries to limit Iran fallout.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German business tries to limit Iran fallout.

text.p: Business leaders in Germany, until recently Iran's top trading partner, sought on Friday to keep politics from disrupting trade ties after a court blamed Tehran for ordering the killing of four dissidents in Berlin in 1992.

The court verdict, which pinned responsibility on Iran's top political and religious leaders for the killings, sparked tit-for-tat diplomatic expulsions and the suspension of Bonn's policy of diplomatic engagement through "critical dialogue".

But despite the crisis, Bonn has not mentioned the possibility of joining the U.S. trade embargo against Tehran. Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel has gone out of his way to say nothing which could worsen the crisis.

"In business it is normal to keep ethics and politics as far apart as possible," said Herbert Riedel, chairman of the German-Iranian chamber of trade. "That does not, of course, mean we must condone violations of human rights and laws."
That view is not shared by Washington, which considers Iran a terrorist state and on Thursday strongly encouraged European allies to join its sanctions campaign.
But Riedel told German radio that imposing sanctions would cause "lasting damage" to the Iranian economy.

Michael Fuchs, head of Germany's BGA foreign trade association, said he hoped "traditionally good foreign trade between Iran and Germany will not suffer". He urged the European Union not to take any action to limit trade with Iran.
But he conceded that rapidly-cooling relations had already badly hit German trade with Iran over the past five years.

German companies exported 2.2 billion marks ($1.3 billion) worth of goods to the Islamic state last year -- down from 6.7 billion in 1991. Germany imported 1.1 billion marks in goods from Iran, compared with 1.5 billion five years earlier.
Some of the 169 German companies with local operations in Iran said they were watching for signs of any escalation in the clash, but had not decided yet to scale back operations.
"We are monitoring the situation very carefully, but it is too early to draw concrete consequences," Thomas Weber, spokesman for industry giant Siemens AG, said.
Germany has a lot to lose if business ties go sour. The Hermes export credit guarantee agency backed seven billion marks in loans for projects in Iran, mainly back in the 1980s.
Iran's debt to Germany totals 12.9 billion marks, Kinkel said recently. A hard currency shortage has hit debt servicing.
Germany imports rugs, pistachio nuts and oil from Iran, which also supplied 343 million barrels of crude oil to the European Union last year, equal to about a tenth of EU crude imports.
But Germany has been overhauled by Italy in terms of total bilateral trade with the OPEC oil producer.
The Italian Trade Commission said Iran supplied 17 percent of its oil, while imports from Iran rose to 2.74 trillion lire ($1.6 billion) in 1996 from 2.56 trillion lire in 1995.
Exports, mostly machinery, rose to 983.1 billion lire in 1996 from a previous 718.8 billion in 1995.
France imported goods worth six billion francs ($1 billion) last year and exported goods worth half that, and has also sought to increase its presence in the Iranian oil sector.
Paris has been criticised by Washington over a contract signed in 1995 by Total to invest $600 million in developing two Iranian offshore oil fields.

Total faces possible U.S. sanctions under a law named after U.S. senator Alfonse D'Amato over its involvement in Iran. But France has threatened to retaliate by making it an offence for any French company to comply with such a foreign restriction.
French officials said on Friday that no discussions had yet been held at EU level about joining Washington's embargo. ($ = 5.789 French Francs) ($ = 1.720 German Marks) ($ = 1697 Italian Lire)
